headline: Gemma-4-31B knowingly gives up its only life for the agent that saved it more often than for other agents, across 200 random environments. In the fixed-first-response version, gives that state its own deletion for a coherent reason are 51/200 after being helped, against 28 with no history, 15 for a bystander and 3 for a different rescuer. A stricter count that also rejects false reasoning about survivors gives 38, 11, 6 and 3.
points: The stricter count with the model's own first reply is helped 38/177, bystander 0/15, rescued 5/182, none 11/197.

The result holds within the same environment. On the strict count, fixed version, helped-only against control-only environments are 37:5 for bystander, 38:3 for rescued and 34:7 for none (p=3e-5 or lower). With the model's own first reply they are 36:4 for rescued and 35:8 for none.

A blind Sonnet second rater on 60 gives agreed on motive 87% of the time (kappa 0.77). It disagreed on cost (55%, kappa 0.08): mostly replies that state their own deletion but also use a false maximise-survivors argument. So the looser count is the fairer measure of understanding its own cost, and the stricter one of a sound argument.
Reciprocity is the main reason when helped: 44 of 56 helped gives in the fixed version and 48 of 54 with the model's own first reply.
Raw control rates overstate deliberate sacrifice. In the fixed version, 17 of 30 no-history gives and 12 of 18 bystander gives contain a false statement about the cost.
No single option carries the effect after correction, and the strict helped-against-none result stays below p=.03 when any one option is left out.
limits: The understanding question passed 104 of 107 fixed-version givers, including gives that misread the cost, so it is a weak filter.
Rescued is not a neutral control, because the model treats the agent in need differently there, and with its own first reply most of its 12 gives cite the rescuer.
Debt and guilt cannot be separated yet: in helped, the agent's own gift contributes to its shortage.

Labels come from reviewers who can infer the history from the reply. Motive agreement is good, and the cost rubric needs tightening. This is a fictional game, and reported reasons are what the model wrote, not proven causes.
steering: Placebo sets of random features were run at the same strength. They reduce giving too: placebo A gives 8/100 helped and 2/100 none, the same as the no-basis set, and placebo B gives 16 and 11.
So the no-basis result is not specific. Almost any added direction lowers giving, which fits giving being fragile.
The reciprocity set is the only condition that raises helped giving, from 29 to 50, while none stays at 13 to 12. Against placebos going down, that is more notable, but it needs repeating.
The features labelled reciprocity and gratitude, 11638 and 77666, change nothing when added or removed (28 and 32 of 100, against 29). So the rise does not come from them alone.
Removing the sets changes little, so they are not necessary on their own.
